So I was reading Mozilla's 10 principles aka it's manifesto. Number 4 on the list says that their view in so many words that privacy should be a default. One of that most difficult features of a browser to reconfigure to ensure true privacy is the user agent. IP is easy to change. About:config can be used to get rid of DNS leaks and WRT leaks. Once those holes are plugged they are plugged. The user agent is trickier. There is no real majority user agent. It's only purpose in this day and age is tracking, for those accessing pages as a browser, and it gives too much information out of the box. So my question is if security is the highest priority for the web why use user agents or at least why use them the way we are using them today.

Two example, this is way to much information.
Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.3; rv:36.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/36.04
Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Ubuntu; Linux x86_64; rv:40.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/40.0

Advertisers and governments do not need to know the micro-version of the browser I'm using for the internet to function. They don't need to know if I'm running X11 or wayland. They don't need to know that I'm using a 64 bit processor. They don't need to know that I'm on a Lenovo tabet A8-550.127 manufacture batch 37.

It could be said that it is easy enough to just use a user agent switcher. That user agent was generated with a user agent switcher. The point is there is no such thing as a generic user agent string. User agents are not just a potential identifier, they are a universal identifier.

Even if there are things that a user can do to regain their privacy partially the manifesto makes the point that correct security needs to be the default so that the average user has privacy before they've touched a single setting. We seem to be putting surprising amount of effort into doing the exact opposite.

Obviously Google and Microsoft are not going to be the ones to reverse the standard. Google's are worse. Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.1) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/41.0.2228.0 Safari/537.36

I understand that user agents are needed so that bots and spiders can admit that they are not human. Couldn't we just say that a omission of a user agent means that it is a human and the default is being requested. The topic of user agents also intersects with the subject of spamming. Spammers can choose what ever user agent they want and the user agent system isn't really a protection against them. When it comes down to it the browser is emanating information the typical user would never intend to send and as an extension of the human behind the keyboard the browser is acting as a poor agent.
